summary:
Long-duration space missions—spanning from Low Earth Orbit (LEO) to future lunar operations and transits to Mars—impose critical challenges on crew health and safety. Faced with Earth-to-space communication latencies that can reach up to 20 minutes, reliance on exclusively ground-based medical support proves unfeasible for addressing physiological emergencies in real time. To meet this operational demand, AstroGuard was developed as an advanced biomedical prototype system for monitoring vital signs and body kinematics, designed to ensure clinical autonomy aboard spacecraft and extraterrestrial habitats.

Developed by Team Los Capa 8, AstroGuard integrates a wearable acquisition node embedded within the astronaut's garment with an artificial intelligence-powered edge analytics processing backend. The system continuously monitors the crew member's physiological and biomechanical profile without compromising mobility or requiring a persistent uplink to the Deep Space Network (DSN).
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?
  • General Operation: AstroGuard is an advanced biomedical and biomechatronic prototype system designed for the autonomous, continuous, and real-time monitoring of crew members' vital signs and body kinematics.
  • Architecture and Processing: It operates via an ESP32 microcontroller that coordinates peripheral sensors (heart rate, SpO2, infrared temperature, and accelerometry) by applying edge digital signal processing (Edge DSP).
  • Artificial Intelligence and Telemetry: Data is structured in JSON format and transmitted locally to a medical console (Flask + SQLite), where an unsupervised AI model (Isolation Forest) detects anomalous patterns and an Ollama-powered copilot assists the user intuitively.
  1. What benefits does it have?
  • Total Clinical Autonomy: By processing data locally at the node and the spacecraft console, it solves the critical problem of space communication latencies (of up to 20 minutes on Mars missions) without relying on Earth.
  • Hardware Resilience: It incorporates contingency plans, such as automatic switching to direct electrocardiography (AD8232) in the event of unforeseen failures in the optical sensors.
  • Ergonomics and Physical Safety: Its physical structure protects against impacts and electromagnetic noise in microgravity using space-grade materials.
  • Clear Operational Guidance: It issues graded alerts and guidance recommendations to facilitate rapid decision-making in warning or danger situations.
  1. What is the intended impact of the project?
  • Space Impact: Contributing to the preservation of astronauts' health, safety, and physical performance during long-duration space missions (Low Earth Orbit, EVA activities, lunar, and Martian missions).
  • Terrestrial Impact: Thanks to its robust and autonomous design, the technology can be effectively adapted to high-risk terrestrial applications and isolated environments, such as monitoring firefighters, mining rescue workers, and emergency medical personnel.
  1. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
  • Hardware:

    • ESP32 Microcontroller (with ULP coprocessor).
    • Sensors: MAX30102 optical module, MLX90614 infrared thermometer, AD8232 analog front-end, and MPU-6050 6-axis inertial measurement unit.
    • Structure and Shielding: NuSil CV-2500 silicone, layers of Kapton, aluminized Mylar, and aerospace-grade PEEK.
    • Python and Flask (for the backend and REST API).
    • Scikit-Learn (to implement the Isolation Forest model).
    • Python wfdb library (to process PhysioNet datasets in Google Colab).
    • Ollama (for the local AI Copilot).
    • CAD modeling environment and SQLite WAL databases.
  1. How is your project creative?
  • Decentralized Edge AI Approach: Combines low-power local monitoring with unsupervised artificial intelligence (Isolation Forest) trained on real PhysioNet biomedical data, successfully detecting anomalies without requiring permanent connection to cloud servers.
  • Modular and Balanced Mechanical Design: Its annular bracelet structure distributes components at $180^\circ$ to balance masses in microgravity, further integrating a multi-layer shielding (Kapton/Mylar/PEEK) that emulates real aerospace mission specifications.
  • Dynamic Adaptability: Capability to hot-reconfigure data acquisition sources upon sensor failures.
  1. What factors did your team consider?
  • Space Environmental Factors: Extreme microgravity conditions, vast communication latencies, and the presence of electromagnetic interference (EMI/RFI).
  • Strict Material Selection: Use of components certified for low outgassing (such as NuSil CV-2500 silicone and PEEK) to prevent toxicity and degradation in closed space cabins.
  • Energy Efficiency: Leveraging the ultra-low-power (ULP) mode of the ESP32 to maintain passive surveillance of critical thresholds and save battery life.
  • Ethical and Clinical Responsibility: Explicitly considering that the system is an experimental prototype for operational support rather than a definitive diagnostic medical device or life-support system.
